name: Anchoring effect
statement: Show someone a number before asking them to estimate a quantity and their estimate moves toward it, even when the number carries no information about the answer.
meaning: The standard demonstration has two steps. First a comparison: is the height of Mount Everest more or less than 45,500 feet? Then an estimate: how high is it? The comparison question plants a figure, and the estimate that follows sits closer to that figure than it would have otherwise. What makes the result strange is that the anchor carries no information. In the founding demonstration the number came off a wheel of fortune spun in front of the participants. Whether an anchor that is visibly random still pulls is contested, and the two meta-analyses cited below disagree about it. Kahneman and Tversky described the mechanism as adjustment: an estimate starts from the number supplied and moves away from it, and it stops too soon.

origin.note: Anchoring is one of three heuristics described in "Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases". The standardised procedure that later work replicates comes from Jacowitz and Kahneman in 1995, which is why the replication below tests their version rather than the 1974 demonstration.

evidence: The 1974 anchoring section is a paragraph long. A number between 0 and 100 came off a wheel of fortune spun in front of the participants, who said whether a quantity was above or below it and then estimated the quantity. Median estimates of the percentage of African countries in the United Nations were 25 and 45 for the groups given 10 and 65. That passage reports no sample size and no test statistic. Jacowitz and Kahneman built the measurable version: a calibration group estimates fifteen quantities unaided, and each anchor is set at the 15th or the 85th percentile of what that group said. Estimates followed the anchor. The Many Labs replication took four of those questions, on the distance from San Francisco to New York, the population of Chicago, the height of Mount Everest and the number of babies born daily in the United States, and ran them across 36 samples.

replication.headline: All four anchoring questions came back across 36 samples, each significant in every sample, and each larger than the 0.93 the original reported.
replication.detail: Many Labs 1 tested thirteen findings across 36 samples and 6,344 participants, 27 collected in a laboratory and nine online. Anchoring was the strongest thing in it. Every one of the four questions reached significance in 100% of samples, in the same direction, with no sample finding nothing and no sample finding the opposite. Unweighted effect sizes were d = 2.60 for babies born, 2.45 for Mount Everest, 2.05 for Chicago and 1.27 for the distance to New York; weighting by sample size lowers each to 2.42, 2.23, 1.79 and 1.17. Eleven of the project's other twelve effects came in below d = 1, and two of them, flag priming and currency priming, did not replicate at all. No later Many Labs project repeated these questions. Many Labs 2 tested a different anchoring paradigm, the text of Many Labs 3 contains no anchoring task, and Many Labs 4 and 5 took up mortality salience and pre-data-collection peer review. A Crossref search in August 2026 of titles containing "Registered Replication Report" returned 36 distinct reports, none of them on anchoring.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152.

limits: The two numbers above are less comparable than they look, and the replication report says so itself. The 1995 paper did not publish enough detail to compute an effect size per question, so its 0.93 is one aggregate figure across all fifteen questions, and it comes from a test-retest design where each participant saw both the anchored and unanchored version. The replication assigned people at random to one anchor or the other, between subjects. Different designs produce different effect sizes for the same underlying phenomenon, so the jump from 0.93 to 2.45 should be read as evidence that the effect is present and large, rather than as a measurement that it grew. The participant count given here is for the Mount Everest question; the other three range from 5,284 to 5,609. And the effect does not survive being weakened. Many Labs 2 tested incidental anchors, where the number is not part of the question at all but sits in the environment: a phone called the P97 versus one called the P17, with participants estimating its sales. The original found d = 0.30 in 207 people, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.58. Across 6,826 people it came back at d = 0.04, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.09, and at the eleven sites that used paper and pencil, the medium the original authors had chosen, it went slightly the wrong way at d = -0.01. So a number attached to the question moves estimates by more than a standard deviation and a number merely nearby moves them by nothing. Shanks, Barbieri-Hermitte and Vadillo ran three studies on Critcher and Gilovich's method and obtained no statistically significant incidental anchoring, while standard anchoring in the same studies held. Schley and Weingarten pooled 2,601 effect sizes from fifty years of anchoring research, 1,280 of them comparing a high anchor against a low one, and report Hedges' g = 0.825, 95% CI 0.765 to 0.884, an effect that survives correction for publication bias. The published abstract renders that point estimate as a formula placeholder and the full text is paywalled, so the figures here are read off the authors' preprint. Their moderator table puts the typical anchoring effect at 0.82, takes 0.72 off it for incidental or primed anchors, 95% CI -0.88 to -0.56, and takes 0.19 off for anchors made transparently random, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.05. Röseler and Schütz, pooling 393 effects from 17,708 people at g = 0.689, 95% CI 0.589 to 0.789, go further and report that anchors communicated as randomly determined had no effect. Their paper is a preprint carrying no journal DOI, and it disagrees with Schley and Weingarten on the point the popular retelling leans on hardest. The self-generated variant, where the estimate starts from a number the participant retrieves rather than one supplied, is a separate paradigm with a separate record. Schley and Weingarten's primary meta-analysis holds no observations of it, because it is not run as a high anchor against a low one. Röseler and colleagues replicated Epley and Gilovich's studies on the distinction and found every experimenter-provided item significant at d of 0.60 or above, against three of six self-generated items in the same study. The 1974 wheel-of-fortune procedure itself appears never to have been directly repeated. Crossref title and bibliographic searches in August 2026 returned no such repeat, and Schley and Weingarten's text mentions the wheel only as the origin of the paradigm. Li, Weigel, Ferraro and Messer add a warning about magnitude. They report that anchoring designs, replication studies included, routinely fail to reach 30% power, and their higher-powered repeat of a bidding experiment found a 3.4% effect, 95% CI -3.4% to 10%, against the 31% the original reported.
misreadings: Anchoring is often described as showing that people are irrational about numbers in general, which overstates it. The effect is about estimates under uncertainty; when someone knows the answer, there is nothing for an anchor to move. It is also frequently attached to advice about opening first in a negotiation, which is not the laboratory case. Schley and Weingarten code a first offer as a directional anchor, because the direction the other side is meant to move in is implied, and directional anchors run 0.66 above the typical effect, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.95. The mechanism is contested even though the effect is not. Insufficient adjustment is Tversky and Kahneman's account, and selective accessibility, where the anchor primes evidence consistent with itself, covers much of the same data. Harris and seven colleagues ran five experiments on what they call the signature test for selective accessibility, four with that test and one with a different method, and found no evidence for it. A robust effect is not the same as a settled explanation.
